ed13e6c9-1b55-5025-a832-f8d710bb6ff1.name: The Mother of God Smolenskaya with Oklad
ed13e6c9-1b55-5025-a832-f8d710bb6ff1.description:
This is a *Hodegetria* (Greek for “one who shows the way”) Mother of God icon, recognizable by the solemn expression of the Mother of God and the frontal position of the Christ Child delivering a blessing. The Christ Child sits on his Mother’s left knee and holds a tightly rolled scroll. The original icon was brought from Byzantium in the 12th century and kept in the Assumption Cathedral in the city of Smolensk. In the 15th century, the icon was transferred to Moscow before being returned to Smolensk.  
This icon has four additional figures, two on each border: a guardian angel and Venerable Basil the Confessor on the left, and Saint John the Baptist and Saint Anne the Prophet on the right. The *oklad* (covering) is solid silver under mercury gilding with no apparent hallmark. The *oklad* has a large nimbus containing sculpted angels with openings for their faces and hands, as well as many gems and a raised floral and fruit design. An inscription on the bottom border reads as follows:  
  
At the Alenskiy-Skete in the area of Kerzhenets, the Schemamonk Filaret the icon painter, had painted this icon for the Schemamonk Iosif. At the year 7250 \[1740\] this icon was given to the treasury of the Schemanun Irinarkha. The Abbess, the nun Anafoliya donated this icon in the year 7376 \[1868\], at the third day of February to the Archbishop Antonij of Moscow and Vladimir.

keywords: Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography

edf3df89-1b5b-56bb-bbe1-38af5be2d483.name: Dress sword of a Landammann
edf3df89-1b5b-56bb-bbe1-38af5be2d483.description: Swords became the favoured weapons of citizens during the age of the French Revolution. A sumptuously designed sword served as a mark of civic distinction. The Landammann (chief official) of Appenzell, Jacob Zellweger-Zuberbühler (1770-1821), acquired this impressive item in Paris. He and his brother were successful merchants based in Trogen in Appenzell Ausserrhoden. Together with his wife and the official delegation of the Swiss Confederation, Jacob travelled to Paris to attend Napoleon’s coronation as emperor in 1804. While there, he took the opportunity to purchase this dress sword from the renowned goldsmith and sword maker Antoine-Modeste Fournera who had its splendid gilt-brass hilt elaborately embossed and engraved. A stylish dragon rests atop the pommel cap; the finish of the scabbard is equally lavish. The blade was made by the Coulaux Brothers in the Alsatian town of Klingenthal between 1801 and 1804; its reverse is marked “Manufacture National de Klingenthal”. The Swiss National Museum acquired this dress sword in 2015 from a Swiss family related to the original owner, Jacob Zellweger-Zuberbühler.

Its two-cylinder V-shaped engine is located in the rear and displaced 565 cubic centimetres, producing 2 horsepower at 1,000 revolutions per minute through a transmission chain drive.

effaa1df-9ca1-5f7e-bc65-9a7edb7a597c.name: Tunic (uniform). Officer in the regiment of Swiss Guards, quartermaster general in Holland.
effaa1df-9ca1-5f7e-bc65-9a7edb7a597c.description: Uniform of Albert Dietegen von Planta from Zuoz (b. 1740, d. March or May 1803), major general and inspector of the Dutch infantry. In 1795, von Planta returned to Switzerland where he acted as deputy to the war council of the Three Leagues (Canton of Grisons). Between 1568 and 1829, a total of 80,000 Swiss troops is estimated to have fought for the Dutch on thirty-one occasions. In 1672, King William III (William of Orange) took into service some 100 Swiss halberdiers as his personal bodyguard, the so-called "Guardes Zwitzers". In the second half of the eighteenth century, Holland had a regiment of Swiss Guards and several Swiss line regiments, largely comprising men from the Protestant canton of Bern, but also from Zurich and Grisons; they were disbanded in 1796. The last four Swiss regiments served in Holland from 1814 until their disbandment in 1829.

f0caab25-464f-52d9-b190-deaa117a11ab.name: Benz Ideal
f0caab25-464f-52d9-b190-deaa117a11ab.description:
Following in the footsteps of the first patented car (Velocipede) by German inventor Carl Benz in 1886, this vehicle represents some of the most cutting edge technology at the dawn of the 20th century. This 1900 Benz Ideal appears as a motorised carriage with wooden details, a leather bench, and an original umbrella.  
  
The water-cooled combustion engine implanted across the back of this automobile achieved a maximum speed of 35km/h with a groundbreaking 4.5 horsepower.  
  
Produced between 1898 and 1902, the Ideal gained popularity in the United Kingdom being imported and sold by Hewetson’s Ltd. This pioneering wagon remains one of the last Benz vehicles without the recognisable “Mercedes” name, legally protected since 1902.

f1f64fbc-60a3-59aa-b153-b3abfce5bf28.name: Willys MB ¼ Ton
f1f64fbc-60a3-59aa-b153-b3abfce5bf28.description:
In early 1940, the United States government began recognising the growing threat posed by Hitler’s Third Reich. With Europe showing signs of vulnerability, America initiated preparations for any eventuality. The war machine was mobilised, but a significant shortfall became evident: the U.S. Army was severely under-equipped in light vehicles suited for the battlefield, with only 30,000 units available. The situation was even more critical for four-wheel-drive vehicles.  
  
In June 1940, William Beasley, chairman of the Technical Committee of the General Staff, drafted specifications for a new quarter-ton 4x4 vehicle for military use. The vehicle was to have a minimum ground clearance of 16 cm, a maximum body length of 2,032mm, and a payload capacity of at least 272kg, enough to carry three men and a machine gun. The total weight was capped at 590kg. Ford developed the Pygmy prototype, whose body shape influenced later Willys MB models. However, Willys-Overland secured production thanks to their superior Willys Quad prototype, powered by the 2.2-litre “Go Devil” engine, an evolution of the 1920s Whippet design. Delivering 60 hp, it enabled speeds of up to 105km/h while maintaining fuel efficiency between 12 and 15 litres per 100km.  
  
One wartime rival to the Willys MB “Jeep” was the Volkswagen Kübelwagen, which performed similar military roles but featured rear-wheel drive and an air-cooled engine. Unlike the Kübelwagen, the Jeep wasn’t the first four-wheel-drive vehicle, but it was the first to be mass-produced at scale. Its compact dimensions and powerful engine allowed it to transport soldiers and light weaponry swiftly to the front lines. By the end of World War II in 1945, around 640,000 Jeep models had been produced, solidifying its legacy as an iconic military vehicle.

f29b84af-a354-519f-abf4-763d9a15df5a.name: White Rumi Dress
f29b84af-a354-519f-abf4-763d9a15df5a.description: Dress made of white, handwoven raw linen, embroidered mostly with red and pink silk. The embroidery is cross-stitch in traditional Ramallah motif and colour pattern. The dress comes with basic long sleeves that show floral motifs under the arms and on the cuffs. Two identical, thick embroidery stripes sit on each side of the waist, with heavy embroidery on the border. One of the most distinguishing features of this dress is the shape of the *qabbeh* (chest panel) and the chevron on it. The chest panel is embroidered with different motifs. The centre of the panel has a chevron topped by two branches of flowers and, under it, two squares of embroidery with feathers on the sides. The panel is framed by flowers and a few feather motifs embroidered on the edges. This dress is considered to be the traditional wedding dress in Ramallah. It is very distinctive because Ramallah is one of few regions that uses white fabric and, even here, white is relatively rare. Some women might also wear this style of dress, but with different stitches, on a daily basis, and this is what makes the Ramallah dress so special. Ramallah is a Palestinian city in the central West Bank, north of Jerusalem, and is generally considered the most affluent and cultural, as well as the most liberal, of all Palestinian cities. Like most Palestinian areas, Ramallah has a rich culture of song, dance and costumes. We see examples of Palestinian attire in artifacts from the Canaanite period. Before the Palestinian Nakba in the 1948 war, traditional costumes for Palestinian women varied regionally in design.

f2c8c673-16bb-5d8a-a1d0-ef90c0a872b5.name: Drawing of Two Fish
f2c8c673-16bb-5d8a-a1d0-ef90c0a872b5.description: In spring 2015, the Swiss National Museum acquired a rare drawing by the Zurich artist Hans Asper (1499–1571). The famous portrait of the Protestant reformer Huldrich Zwingli is another work by him. Here Asper has drawn two species of fish, a trout and an allis shad, and has meticulously captured the detail of their heads. He has signed his work at the right-hand edge and dated it 1540. This realistic drawing is one of the earliest surviving examples of an interest in science that was evolving within the circle around Huldrich Zwingli and Conrad Gessner in Zurich; as such, it is unique in Swiss art history.

f3ee0c5f-372f-5ec0-996c-848dbbcf82e6.name: Mercedes Benz W196 R
f3ee0c5f-372f-5ec0-996c-848dbbcf82e6.description:
The W196 R's first victory coincided with its debut in the 1954 French Grand Prix at Reims, with Juan Manuel Fangio and Karl Kling coming in first and second, respectively. At the wheel of the W196 R, Fangio won the Formula 1 Championship titles in 1954 and 1955.  
Fifteen units were produced, one of which was donated to the Museum in 1957 with a letter from Nallinger, chief engineer of Daimler-Benz, followed by a second one from Alfred Neubauer himself. The W196 R can reach speeds of 290km/h thanks to its eight-cylinder engine, which displaces 2,496 cubic centimetres and provides 290 horsepower at 8,000 revolutions per minute.

f795fd67-bd2c-50a0-87cd-f4f308542324.name: Earth and celestial globe, the so-called 'St. Gallen Globe'
f795fd67-bd2c-50a0-87cd-f4f308542324.description: For many years, the so-called St. Gallen Globe, one of the prized objects of Swiss cultural history, was a source of contention. The globe featuring Mercator maps of the earth and the celestial sphere was created by Tilemann Stella in northern Germany towards the end of the sixteenth century, as a document discovered in 2016 reveals. Although they were not suitable for navigation, globes were extremely popular in the early modern period. What makes the St. Gallen Globe so special is its combination of world and celestial globes. Entitled as a gift, which, however, was later satisfied, the globe was incorporated in the library of the Abbey of St Gallen where it was kept until 1712. During the Second War of Villmergen the globe was robbed and carted off to Zürich where it was displayed in the Wasserkirche (Water Church). St Gallen demanded the return of the globe, but to no avail. When the Swiss National Museum was established in 1898, the globe passed into the hands of the Swiss Confederation; it has been on display in the museum ever since. The dispute over the treasure, which went down in Swiss history as the cultural heritage conflict between Zürich and St Gallen, was only resolved in 2006 when the St Gallen Abbey library received a true copy of the contested globe.

Since then it is in the property of the Stadtbibliothek Zürich, now called Zentralbibliothek. When the Landesmuseum opened its doors in 1898 it was given into possession of the Landesmuseum as part of the “Morgengabe”.

f88098bc-50f7-5ca7-967e-46470db8f2ff.name: Rolls-Royce Silver Ghost
f88098bc-50f7-5ca7-967e-46470db8f2ff.description:
Shortly after the in 1904 partnership between Charles Rolls and Henry Royce and the production of the 30HP model, the Rolls-Royce brand developed a new chassis in 1906 the 40/50HP would be the origin of the Silver Ghost model. Rightly considered in its time the “best car in the world”, the Silver Ghost remained in production, with minor mechanical changes, between 1907 and 1925, reaching a total of 6173 chassis made in England. In 1921, Rolls-Royce opened a manufacturing line in the United States, which lasted until 1926, where a further 1703 chassis were produced – these became known as the Springfield – Silver Ghost.  
  
The name "Silver Ghost" came about as the nickname for a demonstration car, commissioned in 1907 by Claude Johnson, Rolls-Royce’s Commercial and Marketing Director. Intended to advertise the British brand, the original model had bodywork by Barker in the “Roi-des-Belges” style and was painted in shades of aluminium. The “Silver Ghost” suggested not only quiet running but also smooth rolling. During the First World War, Rolls-Royce stopped development of the model, supplying only the mechanicals for military use. This Rolls-Royce Silver Ghost, chassis number 1707, in the Museu do Caramulo collection, was the first to be imported to Portugal by the brand’s dealer in Lisbon, José Rugeroni, who sold it to an Englishman, Frank Pidwell, who lived in Santiago do Cacém. He registered it on 17 November 1911 with registration number S-323.

f8cd3f1c-9fcc-5090-8b81-3fc07e4812f5.name: Autocar M3 Half-Track
f8cd3f1c-9fcc-5090-8b81-3fc07e4812f5.description:
Determined to improve the mobility of its troops in the late 1920s, the American army acquired several Citroën-Kégresse models for a benchmark study. Unmistakably distinct for using tracks instead of rear wheels, these models came into their own on rough terrain, where normal cars struggled. Under the supervision of the US Department of Military Material, several prototypes were built, which later gave rise to the famous M2 and M3 models.  
  
Built by the Autocar Company, Diamond T Motor Company and the White Company, the models were extensively tested on civil roads, to improve service conditions as well as reliability. The engines, the White 160AX and the IHC Red Diamond 450, were coupled to an unsynchronized manual gearbox with four speeds and a transfer gearbox with two ratios.  
  
Boasting a more imposing body than its M2 sibling, the M3 half track was designed for use in multiple war scenarios, but its main function was to transport troops. Measuring 6.52 meters in length with ten seats at the rear and three more in the cabin, the M3 also carried ammunition and weaponry behind the seats. External supports were often added to carry groceries, backpacks and other items out of necessity. Built in July 1943, by the Autocar Motor Company, this M3 half track with registration number USA 4065552/S was one of 43,000 units registered by the US Army. This very M3 saw front line action during the Second World War.

f8ef1a5d-bd50-58f0-8924-3cf66022bfda.name: Inauguration of the Grande Dixence dam
f8ef1a5d-bd50-58f0-8924-3cf66022bfda.description: The water level is shown here rising behind the Grande Dixence dam near Sion (Valais), 18/07/1957; image from the feature produced by the Presse Diffusion Lausanne (PDL) photo agency. Constructed between 1950 and 1964, and commissioned between 1961 and 1965, the dam is located in the Valais commune of Hérémence. The crest of the dam lies at an altitude of 2,365 metres above sea level; this makes the dam Switzerland’s highest-lying construction. The dam wall is 285 metres high, making it the world’s tallest gravity dam. A symbol of Swiss engineering excellence, the Grande Dixence dam is the biggest producer of sustainable energy in Switzerland today. The 1950s and 1960s represented a period of economic and social advancement in Switzerland, and press photographers recorded the changes in full and in detail. Those working for the PDL and Actualités Suisses Lausanne (ASL) agencies focused particularly on the construction boom in the energy and transport sectors, and often also on the societal and political debates, conflicts, and repercussions associated with it. The Swiss National Museum acquired the PDL and ASL archives in 2007. Combined they number around six million images in the form of negatives, prints, and slides. Covering the years from 1937 to 1999, they record the most significant developments during the era of analogue press photography.

f9a18ff2-f597-5b8b-bbfe-3e66d75ad509.name: Beit Dajan Wedding Dress
f9a18ff2-f597-5b8b-bbfe-3e66d75ad509.description: Black dress made of black linen fabric. The chest panel of the dress is framed on three sides with different colours, surrounding a *tashreefa* motif. It has a V-neck collar with tassels, and is embellished with lulu braid work that has flowers on both ends. The neck and shoulders are made of wine-coloured linen fabric with a thick orange lacing. The sleeves include *hirmizi* fabric with multiple colours of embroidery and framed by lulu braid work with flowers. The back panel of the dress shows flowers on two sides with an oval in the centre. The *banayeq* (side panels) include soft floral motifs with geometrical shapes, surrounded by trim in geometrical motifs. A lulu braid work with flowers is seen on the centre of the front panel, while the back shows horizontal braid work of cypress trees and vertical braid work similar to the front panel. This dress is representative of garments from Beit Dajan, a Palestinian village located to the east of Nablus. Beit Dajan is famous for its fertile agricultural land, which may be a great source of inspiration for the embroidery on this garment. The women of Beit Dajan village embroider and sew this type of garment on their own, and they wear it on occasions and celebrations like weddings. It is not suitable for daily life as it is heavy and ornate.

fb6d76a4-8c2e-5feb-8110-649d35ff03da.name: Celestial globe
fb6d76a4-8c2e-5feb-8110-649d35ff03da.description: As everyone knows, 29 February is a leap day and appears on the calendar only once every four years. The day was introduced in 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII. The new Gregorian calendar finally did justice to the fact that a year has 365.2425 days. Only four years later, Jost Bürgi, a brilliant astronomer, mathematician, clockmaker, and maker of astronomical instruments, built a celestial globe incorporating the new calendar for the German Kaiser. He developed the first-ever mechanical system to display 29 February in leap years. Bürgi was born in what is today the canton of St. Gallen and worked with the famous astronomer Johannes Kepler at the imperial court in Prague. In addition to the celestial globe, he also invented many other things. He was the first person to draw up a logarithmic table. Additionally, he built a clock with three hands, thereby creating the second as a unit of time.

fca64e61-e845-5774-ac1f-daa9aaafc242.name: Mercedes Benz 600
fca64e61-e845-5774-ac1f-daa9aaafc242.description:
This signature vehicle stands out as the “Grand Mercedes” – the world’s most expensive car at the time of its launch. Finished in glossy black paint, the 600 “Sonderklasse” (German for “special class”) was manufactured to carry eminent icons.  
  
The presidential model of this limousine would carry world-leaders like Queen Elizabeth II, Kim Il-sung and former Yugoslavian president Josip Broz Tito. The design with a chauffeur screen-divider would attract other famous personalities like Elizabeth Taylor, Pablo Escobar, Coco Chanel, Elvis Presley, and David Bowie.  
  
With appearances in popular movies like James Bond, the forerunner of today’s Maybach surpassed Rolls-Royce, Bentley and the Imperial in luxury and technology.

fe542c7b-3a57-5753-bfe2-3d0c265edc3e.description: Max Fröhlich attended metalworking classes at the Zurich School of Arts and Crafts together with Max Bill during the 1920s. A key representative of modernism, Fröhlich developed a functional style characterized by clarity of form. Besides engraving and enamelling, he mainly used casting techniques to express his concept of form. In the 1970s, Fröhlich tested the limits of jewellery by designing pieces made with electrical cable.

ffa8bb2b-6412-5238-b1e9-19ae24e65029.name: Parting scene
ffa8bb2b-6412-5238-b1e9-19ae24e65029.description: On St. Berchtold’s day in 1801, the family gathered around Johann Caspar Lavater’s deathbed and said their farewells to the famous pastor of St. Peter’s church in Zurich. He died on January 2, 1801 of a gunshot wound received from a French soldier in September 1799 whilst trying to help soldiers injured during the capture of Zurich by General Masséna. His wife Anna Schinz, his brother Diethelm, his two daughters Anna, (the elder) with her husband Georg Gessner, and Louise, and son Heinrich Lavater with his wife Anna Barbara Ott are all gathered by his deathbed.
